Q: How can I fetch an unmerged pull request for a branch I don't own? A:

Once you added the upstream repository as an upstream remote (as Elias pointed out):

git remote add upstream git@github.com:Particular/NServiceBus

You can configure Git (version control) to fetch pull requests by default:

git config --local --add remote.upstream.fetch '+refs/pull/*/head:refs/remotes/upstream/pr/*'

So, let's fetch it:

git fetch upstream

Output:

Fetching upstream
remote: Counting objects: 4, done.
remote: Compressing objects: 100% (2/2), done.
remote: Total 4 (delta 2), reused 4 (delta 2), pack-reused 0
Unpacking objects: 100% (4/4), done.
From https://github.com/Particular/NServiceBus
 * [new ref]         refs/pull/1/head -> upstream/pr/1
 * [new ref]         refs/pull/2/head -> upstream/pr/2

And check it out:

git checkout pr/2

Output:

Branch pr/2 set up to track remote branch pr/2 from upstream.
Switched to a new branch 'pr/2'

Q: How can I check out a GitHub pull request with Git? A:

I accidentally ended up writing almost the same as provided by git-extras. So if you prefer a single custom command instead of installing a bunch of other extra commands, just place this git-pr file somewhere in your $PATH and then you can just write:

git pr 42

# Or
git pr upstream 42

# Or
git pr https://github.com/peerigon/phridge/pull/1

Q: Visual Studio Code Intellisense is very slow - Is there anything I can do? A:

There are a few tools VSCode provides out of the box:

  1. Similar to @MadMac's Answer, you can use the built-in "Start Extension Bisect" under the "Help" Menu or you can find it by typing "bisect" into the command palette

  2. If you have a manageable amount of extensions you can open the "Extensions" tab in the sidebar and filter them by "@installed". Scrolling through the list, you should be able to see a millisecond value in the top right corner of some extensions, this is their startup speed. Disabling extensions with long startup times may also improve VSC's start up speed.

Q: How to intercept HTTPS traffic on machine without proxy? A:

I'll be honest, I don't know exactly how the commercial HTTP debugger implement their proxyless capture. They don't publish it. But there are basically two families of approach on Windows, and one of them is what we use in Fluxzy, so I can describe that one in detail.

Disclosure first: I work on Fluxzy, which mitm engine is open source, so take this as a "here's how it actually works under the hood" answer rather than a pitch.

Basically , there are two approaches

The first is a WFP callout driver. You write a kernel-mode driver on top of the Windows Filtering Platform, sit at the transport layer, and redirect connections before they leave the machine. This is the lowest-level option and it's what a lot of the Windows-only "no proxy" tools use. It's powerful but it means shipping and signing a kernel driver, and it's Windows specific.

The second is a TUN-based approach. Instead of a callout driver you create a virtual network interface, push a route so the system sends packets to it, and read the raw IP packets in user space. On Windows the usual building block for this is wintun, the TUN driver from the WireGuard project. It's a signed kernel driver, but the point is you don't write any kernel code yourself, it just hands packets to userspace through a simple ring-buffer API. This is cross platform in spirit, the same idea works on Linux and macOS with their own TUN devices.

Fluxzy uses the second one. Here is the actual flow.

How the TUN + SOCKS5 path works

  1. We bring up a TUN interface and adjust the routing table so traffic is sent to it. No app needs an HTTP_PROXY variable, no system proxy setting changes. From the application's point of view it just connects to the server normally.
  2. What arrives on the TUN interface is raw IP packets, not HTTP. So we run a tun2socks layer that reassembles the TCP/UDP flows out of those packets and turns each connection into a SOCKS5 connection. (A good tun2socks library I've tested my self will be like https://github.com/heiher/hev-socks5-tunnel , it supports DNS mapping)
  3. That SOCKS5 connection points at Fluxzy's own local SOCKS5 endpoint. So now we're back on familiar ground: we have a real stream, we know the original destination (SOCKS5 carries it), and we can do the normal MITM, generate a leaf cert for the SNI, decrypt TLS, parse HTTP, re-encrypt, forward. So the "no proxy" magic is really just: route at the OS level instead of asking each app to opt in, then convert the captured packets back into something a normal MITM proxy can chew on.

Q: Why do I get different results when running the same code with the same input data? A:

To elaborate more, from my basic experience with training LSTM model for some finance application for predicting if the price of some stock will go up or down, You want your model to be non-predictable in the production, not while you are training/development phase, so here is a logical explanation of why you need to set the seed:

Suppose that I have X_train, which is the training data, and I want to start the training process, after training finishes, I want to analyze the predictions and see if they are good or not based on some conventions related to finance that is out the scope of this discussion, so I will skip it.

Multiple choices, configurations, and parameters values during the training yields different predictions qualities, for example, let's consider which scaling methodology is the best for our finance problem.

I want to try two scaling methodologies; RobustScaler() and MinMaxScaler() scaler. then I want to compare the the prediction results, was the prediction results better when I used MinMaxScaler(), or was the prediction results better when I used RobustScaler() ? So you must run the training process two times, once with RobustScaler() and once with MinMaxScaler(), but there is a catch, you want the same inputs to trigger the same output every time, so for the comparison to be fair, you must keep the training environment Identical for both scalers, otherwise the comparison is not fair, and you will choose worse scaling method instead of choosing better scaler method that would have yielded better results, and the SEED is the thing that makes the environment identical for each design choice.

Q: Render HTML elements simultaneously A:
  • Give them visibility: hidden (or similar) initially and overwrite that using a tag that comes after them in the HTML code:
    • a <script> tag
    • or a <style> tag
    • or for example <span class="young-sibling"> that will trigger :has(+ .young-sibling) { visibility: visible; }
  • or create those elements programmatically in a single <script> instead of including them in the HTML code.

For elements such as <img> and <iframe>, you may additionally want to wait for the load event of each of them. For example, if you want to show such an element simultaneously with one that doesn't have a load event, you have to choose the option above of overwriting visiblity with <scipt> and wait both for that <scipt> to get reached as well as the load event to occur before making them visible.
